    #4258. Industry News: ​2027 Prediction: Security Will Shed Its Reputation As The Bottleneck

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (982 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: ​2027 Prediction: Security Will Shed Its Reputation As The Bottleneck

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Prashanth Harshangi is co-founder of Enkrypt AI, building security and governance infrastructure for enterprise AI deployments.
    • Recent findings suggest that security has a reputation problem.
    • I predict that in 2027 this reputation will flip.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Prashanth Harshangi is co-founder of Enkrypt AI, building security and governance infrastructure for enterprise AI deployments.

    Recent findings suggest that security has a reputation problem. Ask almost any engineering leader what slows down an AI agent rollout, and you’ll hear some version of “waiting on security.”.

    I predict that in 2027 this reputation will flip. Security never slowed transformation. The real blocker is not knowing the answers to basic questions: Where does this agent run? What data can it reach? Who approved its tools, and what happens if one of them changes?

    It has been revealed that when no one can answer quickly, projects stall. A recent research report from Anaconda found that two-thirds of respondents had a deployment delayed by security concerns. Builders wait while security scrambles to reconstruct answers that should have existed from day one, until each side decides the other is the problem.

    Recent findings suggest that the real bottleneck is missing evidence, visibility and shared tooling. In 2027, organizations that build security into the foundation will turn it from a gate into what lets teams move faster with confidence.

    A typical multi-week security review is mostly evidence-gathering: an inventory of models, versions, tools and data sources; testing against adversarial prompts and data leakage; and documentation mapped to frameworks like the NIST AI RMF or the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

    That evidence takes the form of concrete artifacts: an up-to-date inventory of AI components, red teaming results tied to a specific build, logs of what an agent accessed and when and a record of which policies are enforced at runtime.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2027, more organizations will automate this work. When evidence is generated continuously in the pipeline, the review shrinks from weeks of archaeology to a short conversation about the few risks that need human judgment.

    AI intensifies the speed-versus-security debate for two reasons.

    First, the software supply chain now has a second layer of models, MCP servers and agent skills, often pulled in within a single afternoon. Many organizations track code dependencies carefully but can’t say which MCP servers their agents call. I expect the next wave of incidents to start with those untracked assets.

    It has been revealed that the early record already points that way. At our organization, we maintain the Agent Incident Registry (AIR), a public database of 570 source-verified security and safety events involving AI agents from 2022 to 2026. In 219 of them, a real party suffered real consequences, not just a researcher proving an attack was possible.

    Second, agents can act as an insider that is neither human nor malicious. Picture a support agent connected to a customer database through an MCP server. A ticket arrives containing hidden instructions, and the agent follows them, pulling records it was never meant to share into its reply. Nothing was hacked in the traditional sense. The agent used permissions it already had, in a way no one anticipated.

    In a recent development, the most useful mental model I’ve found, and one I expect leading organizations to adopt in 2027, is to treat an AI agent like a upcoming hire. It gets an identity, a named human owner, a documented purpose and an approved tool list before it touches production. It receives the minimum permissions its job requires, scoped to the task and time-bound, never a copy of its owner’s full access. When it’s retired, its credentials are revoked and its activity record is preserved.

    It has been revealed that static, role-based permissions can’t keep up with agents that choose tools at runtime and act on someone else’s behalf. Authorization will have to become contextual: What is this agent trying to do, for whom, right now—and is that within policy?

    According to recent reports, and when something goes wrong, “the AI did it” isn’t an answer. The human owner is accountable for the agent’s scope, the platform team for its controls and the organization for its policy.

    In a recent development, guardrails feel like a tax when they arrive late, block without explanation and require a ticket to get past. They feel like infrastructure when they’re built into the platform and tell developers why something was stopped and how to fix it.

    My test is whether the secure way is also the easiest. If a developer can spin up an agent with preapproved models, vetted MCP servers and default guardrails in the time it takes to wire things up manually, most will choose the secure path without being asked.

    In 2027, I expect automated red teaming in CI, configurable runtime guardrails and self-updating inventories to move security work out of the review meeting and into the tooling.

    Toolchain checks will join them. Every MCP server and agent skill should be scanned before an agent can call it, the same way code dependencies are scanned before a merge.

    That same report from Anaconda found that only 26% of teams reported having a highly unified AI toolchain. In 2027, having experienced the drawbacks of a disparate stack, the most effective CISOs, CTOs and CPOs will stop treating AI security as a handoff between teams and start treating it as a shared product.

    That means shared metrics, such as time from agent prototype to approved production, tracked alongside incident and policy-violation rates. It means a single inventory of models, tools and agents that both teams trust and security engineers embedded with builders from the first design discussion, not the last review. And it means policies expressed as automated checks, so they stop being debates and become part of the build.

    The organizations with the fewest controls won’t win the race. The winners will build controls into their infrastructure, so that shipping a secure agent is simply the default.

    Industry observers note that forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
